common_name: Esopus Spitzenburg Apple (Thomas Jefferson's Favorite Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Esopus Spitzenburg is a light, somewhat biennial bearer and benefits from thinning and a vigorous rootstock to encourage more consistent annual crops.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating in Esopus, New York in the 1700s, this heirloom became famous as the reported favorite eating apple of Thomas Jefferson, who planted it at Monticello. The bright red-orange fruit, dotted with pale russet, has firm, yellow, intensely rich and spicy-sweet flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all apples, though the tree can be a shy, uneven bearer compared to modern commercial varieties. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well in cold storage, developing more complexity over several weeks.
sources: Monticello — Thomas Jefferson's Garden and Orchard

common_name: Roxbury Russet Apple (Oldest Documented American Apple Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Roxbury Russet is vigorous and productive, and its thick russeted skin gives the fruit outstanding storage life compared to smooth-skinned apples.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. First recorded in Roxbury, Massachusetts in the 1630s, this is the oldest apple cultivar documented as having originated in North America, predating the country itself by well over a century. The medium, dull yellow-green fruit is almost entirely covered in rough golden-brown russet, with firm, crisp, sweet-tart flesh well suited to fresh eating, cider, and long winter storage, since the thick skin sheds moisture slowly and resists shriveling. It ripens in mid-fall and was historically prized precisely because it kept so well through the winter months before refrigeration existed.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

common_name: Yellow Transparent Apple (Very Early Translucent-Skinned Russian Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Transparent ripens extremely early, often by late June to early July, and fruit should be used quickly since it bruises easily and does not keep.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Introduced from Russia in the 1870s, Yellow Transparent is one of the earliest-ripening apples grown in North America, producing pale, almost translucent yellow-green skin over soft, tart, juicy flesh that cooks down quickly into a smooth sauce. Because the thin skin bruises easily and the fruit does not store, it is best picked directly for immediate use in pies, sauce, and fresh eating rather than for the fruit bowl. The tree is notably cold-hardy and productive, and its extremely early ripening has long made it a favorite for the first homemade applesauce of the year.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

common_name: Grimes Golden Apple (West Virginia Heirloom Parent of Golden Delicious)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Grimes Golden is a reliable annual bearer and a useful pollinator for many other apple varieties.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Discovered as a chance seedling on Thomas Grimes' farm in Brooke County, West Virginia in the early 1800s, this heirloom is historically significant as the presumed parent of Golden Delicious, one of the most commercially important apples of the 20th century. The medium, deep yellow fruit has dense, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh with a wine-like richness that many old-apple enthusiasts consider superior to its more famous offspring. It ripens in early-to-mid fall and was historically valued both fresh and for cider, keeping reasonably well in a cool cellar.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

common_name: Wolf River Apple (Giant Wisconsin Heirloom Baking Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Wolf River produces unusually large fruit, so thin clusters to a single apple to prevent limb breakage and improve size further.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating near the Wolf River in Fremont, Wisconsin in the mid-1800s, this heirloom is famous chiefly for the sheer size of its fruit, with individual apples sometimes weighing over a pound and reportedly large enough that a single apple can fill a whole pie. The pale yellow-green skin blushed with red covers soft, mild, mellow flesh that is better suited to baking and sauce than fresh eating, since the flavor is pleasant but unremarkable on its own. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and vigorous, and its dramatic fruit size has kept it a curiosity and conversation piece in heirloom orchards for generations.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste
